title: CBOR
subtitle: Canonical CBOR encodes the vector store's RPC wire and the extraction specifications, so equal specifications are byte-identical.

stats.label: RPC variants in the vector store's service API
families they fall into, search among them

lede: Inference Fabric's Vector Shard Manager needed a wire that carries small structured requests and large binary vector payloads in the same frame. I chose CBOR, length-prefixed over TCP to mirror the framing of the fabric's broker protocol, through the ciborium Rust library. Inference Fabric also runs hidden-state extraction, and each run is described by a spec that tells the GPU worker which layer's states to capture and how. Producers attach the spec to every work item and the broker carries it opaquely. I wanted two equal specs to be the same bytes wherever they were produced, so the spec is encoded as canonical, deterministic CBOR, and the mining tables store spec identifiers derived from that encoding.
quote: I use canonical encoding wherever bytes stand for identity.
evidence: Binary wire protocol design: a length-prefixed CBOR wire for a vector store with 33 RPC variants in 6 families, carrying structured fields and binary vectors in one frame with no base64 step.
Canonical encoding and content identity: hidden-state extraction specs encoded as canonical CBOR so equal specs are byte-identical and their identifiers match wherever they were produced.
author: Corey James
